title: Republicans’ midterm reckoning comes for the RNC
summary: President Donald Trump’s handpicked chair is fending off a challenge from his own colleague as Republicans grapple with who should pay the price for midterm losses.
content: The chair of the Republican National Committee is scrambling to avoid becoming the party’s midterms scapegoat. With President Donald Trump’s backing, Joe Gruters would normally be a lock to retain his position as RNC chair. But after this month’s brutal midterm losses, he is now trying to fend off an upstart and surprisingly strong challenge from co-chair KC Crosbie ahead of the January leadership election. As both candidates jockey behind the scenes for support, deep divisions have emerged between members over who bears responsibility for the wipeout earlier this month and what comes next. Party leaders have been reluctant to publicly point fingers at Trump and his unpopular agenda. Instead, conversations with more than two dozen RNC members and operatives familiar with the committee’s dynamics reveal that some are channeling their frustration toward Gruters. Even as his supporters argue he’s being unfairly blamed for a difficult political environment, Gruters could still become the fall guy. For some of Gruters’ critics, the decision is simple: Someone must pay for the once-unthinkable losses. “It is time for new leadership. That's nothing against Joe at all,” said Kentucky GOP Chair Robert Benvenuti, who plans to vote for Crosbie. “But different times require different leadership, different types of leaders.” An undecided RNC member added: “There's an awful lot of anger.” That member, granted anonymity to speak candidly about private conversations, described members questioning whether to “rubber stamp the guy that rightly or wrongly is seen as the architect of this mess.” The debate within the RNC — whether to break with the Trump-backed candidate or stick with the status quo — mirrors the broader reckoning underway in the GOP over how closely to align with the president moving forward. Many Republicans have resigned themselves to Trump’s continued dominance over the next two years, but some RNC members have already begun to agitate for change in other ways, including by calling for an autopsy of the midterms and for congressional leadership elections to be delayed. Several RNC members said Gruters helped the committee raise millions this cycle, arguing that alone is a key part of his job and he handled it well. Others were frustrated that the RNC didn’t engage or spend money in their states earlier. And some members criticized Gruters for allowing the RNC to become overly enmeshed in the White House’s political operation. “The party raised a lot of money, and we spent it. I don't think that there's a whole lot of that that can be laid at [Gruters’] feet,” said West Virginia GOP chair Josh Holstein, who said he has not yet committed either way in the leadership race. “At the same time, I know there's a lot of members of the committee that feel we need to go a different direction, and that the RNC needs to be a little more autonomous in its decision making.” The RNC and Crosbie declined to comment. The White House did not respond to a request for comment. The Gruters campaign said in a statement that RNC members “are rallying behind Chairman Gruters because they know he will never stop fighting for Republicans.” “Chairman Joe Gruters has 25 years of experience at every level of the Republican Party, shattering fundraising records, building the largest election integrity operation in party history, and advancing President Trump’s agenda,” the campaign said. The outcome of the leadership race, which will be determined by a secret ballot, will test just how far RNC members are willing to go to change course — even if it means defying Trump. And the stakes are enormous, with the RNC playing a key role in the presidential race, including running the GOP primary debates, hosting the party’s 2028 convention and supporting the eventual nominee. Complicating the calculation is Trump’s own involvement: The president has been a vocal supporter of Gruters and has privately suggested that if Crosbie wins the leadership battle, he wouldn’t assist the RNC with fundraising ahead of 2028, according to two people familiar with the threat who were granted anonymity to speak about private details. The threat was first reported by Axios . It’s an apparent acknowledgement that even Trump knows it’s a real contest — and that his chosen candidate may become a scapegoat. Vice President JD Vance, who also serves as the RNC’s finance chair and is considering a presidential bid, has privately offered to assist Gruters’ reelection campaign, according to a person with direct knowledge of the outreach granted anonymity to speak about private details. Gruters has not yet taken Vance up on his offer, the person said. Vance’s office did not respond to a request for comment. “There is an element that is concerned about this underlying President Trump support, and if we don’t vote for his guy, we’re undermining the president and further giving him more bad news, black eyes, and there’s some sensitivities to that,” said a second RNC member who is undecided about the leadership election and granted anonymity to speak candidly about sensitive political dynamics. “But you also have some that are more protective of the brand and the party than they are to the person, especially given the results of this last election cycle,” the person said. Trump allies have been checking in with RNC members to gauge where they stand in the leadership race, said the RNC member, who received such a call. It’s not yet clear where the membership stands. Both Gruters’ and Crosbie’s camps are keeping their whip counts closely guarded in part to avoid a repeat of the 2022 RNC chair election, when allies seeking to oust former chair Ronna McDaniel aggressively badgered party members in hopes of elevating Harmeet Dhillon. “I think it's going to be a close race,” said Holstein, the West Virginia GOP chair. Behind the scenes, both candidates have been courting RNC members. Gruters has called people to solicit their support and leaned on both Trump’s endorsement and the consequences of Trump pulling out of future RNC fundraising. Rhode Island GOP Chair Allyn Meyers said Gruters sent him and the state’s other RNC members the president’s Truth Social post giving him his “complete and total endorsement.” “You don’t fire your best salesman because he’s got a bad quarter,” said Illinois GOP chair Bob Grogan, who plans to support Gruters. Crosbie, for her part, has sent a 10-12 page detailed survey to RNC members asking specific questions about the timing of when resources were deployed to their state this cycle and about staffing, among other areas, according to three people familiar with the survey. In conversations with undecided party members, Crosbie has pledged greater transparency into the party’s finances, one of the people said. She is also making her case to members who are frustrated by the party’s perhaps too close coordination with Trump world and want to have greater say in the RNC’s strategy. The RNC has historically operated as a political arm of the president whenever a Republican is in the White House. “You want the coordination, you want the closeness and the efficiency of it,” said Washington GOP chair Jim Walsh, who did not share who he’d be supporting in January. However, he added: “You want those two to be two different heads, two different brains, two different hearts, and you want a little tension there because you riff off each other on how you should proceed on a campaign or on a cycle strategy.” A national GOP strategist who supports Gruters pushed back on the calls for a more independent RNC. “This is not Model UN. It’s about winning elections,” said the person, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. Whether they plan to vote for Gruters, Republican Party chairs from red and blue states alike told POLITICO the midterm results raise the need for a serious reckoning over the role the RNC should play in future cycles — and how it appeals to a broader swath of the electorate. “Regardless of who the chair is, I think there has to be changes in the way the committee operates,” said Ben Proto, Connecticut’s GOP chair, who did not share who he would be supporting in January. “The committee has to look beyond those, you know, in 2024, it was the seven states. In 2026, it was the highly targeted areas. I think we have to broaden our approach to the electorate. We have to look at 50 states.” “We took a pretty good beating two weeks ago or so,” said Benvenuti, of Kentucky. “And in my view, that should cause deep reflection about how the organization should be run, how messaging should be done, how the organization should function internally.” Lauren Fedor contributed reporting.
authors: By Aaron Pellish, Erin Doherty and Andrew Howard
